title: The common good
hookLine: the aims of the law: protect religion, life, mind, lineage and property

cards: Pork is forbidden in the Qur'an. So is meat from an animal that died on its own.
Then, in the very same passage of Surah al-Baqarah, comes an exception: whoever is driven by necessity, not wanting it and not going beyond the limit, carries no sin.
A person starving in the desert with nothing else to eat is not breaking the law by eating. The rule bends, and the text itself bends it. Why would a law make room against its own prohibition?
Because, jurists say, the law has aims, and keeping a person alive is one of them. Today's word is the good those aims protect.

teach.h: MASLAHAH: THE GOOD OF A THING.
teach.b: The word is maslahah: benefit, welfare, the good of a thing. Muslim jurists asked a large question with it: what is the law for?
The scholar al-Ghazali, in his book on legal theory, al-Mustasfa, gave an answer later writers took up.

The law, he wrote, aims to protect five things for people: their religion, their life, their mind, their lineage, and their property. Whatever protects those, he called maslahah; whatever harms them, its opposite.
Run the five through some familiar rules. Prayer and fasting guard religion. The law of retaliation for killing guards life.
The ban on intoxicants guards the mind. The rules of marriage guard lineage, who belongs to whom. The penalty for theft guards property.
Each rule has a job, and the jobs explain the exceptions: that's why the starving person may eat, because a food rule gives way when life itself is at stake.
The Qur'an puts the spirit plainly, in Surah al-Baqarah: "Allah desireth for you ease; He desireth not hardship for you."
Later, the Andalusian scholar al-Shatibi, of the Maliki school, built a whole study on these aims, the maqasid. Now the honest part.

teach.h: HOW FAR CAN IT GO ALONE?
teach.b: The schools agree that the law serves people's good. They differ on how far maslahah can go on its own, where no text speaks. The Maliki school is known for using it more freely.
Others insist it stay tied to a text, so that nobody's private sense of the common good starts writing law. Even the argument is about protecting the same five things.

how: Muslim jurists and teachers often explain rulings by the aims of the law, the protection of religion, life, mind, lineage and property, and the schools differ on how far the common good can be used where no text speaks.

o: the good the law's aims protect, like life and mind
whatever the majority of people happen to want
a rule that bends whenever life gets hard

games.q: which aim does the rule guard — tap the pairs.

s: the Qur'an forbids pork with no exception at all
the same passage excuses the one driven by necessity, not wanting it and not going beyond the limit.
al-Ghazali named five things the law aims to protect
religion, life, mind, lineage and property, in his al-Mustasfa.
every school uses the common good freely where no text speaks
the Maliki school is known for using it more freely; others keep it tied to a text.

games.q: you're lost in the desert, starving, and the only food is meat the Qur'an forbids. what does the passage say?
o: eat, and the sin is forgiven later.
eat: whoever is driven by necessity carries no sin.
don't eat: the rule never bends.
games.why: the text itself makes the exception, for one not wanting it and not going beyond the limit. keeping a life is one of the law's aims.

practice: Choose any rule you live under, religious or not: a speed limit near a school, not leaving a child alone near water, fasting rules that let the sick eat.
Trace it to a life it keeps safe, a face if you can, and let the rule look a little less like a fence and a little more like a hand.
